instruction: Create a single-page SVG showcase of an Indian auto rickshaw (tuk-tuk). Make the vehicle the dominant focal object and visibly include its three-wheel structure, enclosed passenger cabin, driver windshield, canopy roof, headlamp, mirrors, handlebars, mudguards, and small ornamental details. Use convincing three-quarter perspective, layered shading, and a lively street-inspired palette. Put strong emphasis on a coherent composition, precise vector craft, dimensionality, and polished finish.

history.critique: The 'vector study' framing (eyebrow, serif title, numbered callouts) gives the piece a real editorial identity, and the vehicle is clearly the dominant focal object with all required parts present. Weaknesses by pressure: (1) Brief & Intent — the 'small ornamental details' are nearly absent (only a row of rivet dots and a stray thin loop that reads as an artifact, not a tassel), and the 'lively street-inspired palette' is muted by the near-black brown stage; the driver's interior is a muddy dark blob, so the enclosed cabin reads as a box rather than a habitable space. (2) Clarity & Hierarchy — callout 7 'Mudguards' is clipped at the bottom edge; a long stray gray leader line crosses the entire canvas without a clear target; most labels float without consistent connector dots, so number-to-part mapping relies on proximity; the hard-edged tan spotlight ellipse behind the vehicle reads as a misplaced shape and competes with the focal object. (3) Visual System & Craft — the three-quarter perspective is inconsistent: wheels are perfect circles (should be slightly elliptical), the far-side rear wheel's thin mudguard arc is misaligned with its tire, the canopy's left edge doesn't meet the windshield frame cleanly, the handlebars render as an illegible black scribble, and the cabin windows are flat rectangles with no depth. (4) Expressiveness — the vehicle lacks characteristic Indian street ornamentation (no painted motifs, garlands, bells, or trim), so it reads as a generic schematic rather than a tuk-tuk; the only memorable moment is the headlamp glow. Real trade-offs: the annotation layer adds clarity but currently clutters and clips the composition; the dark studio background supports the 'study' mood but suppresses the requested street liveliness; simple flat geometry keeps the vector clean but undermines the requested dimensionality.
history.suggestion: One prioritized plan: 1) Remove jank first — delete the stray diagonal line, replace the hard-edged spotlight with a soft radial glow (or remove it), reposition the vehicle and labels so callout 7 and all wheels sit fully inside the canvas, and add a soft elliptical contact shadow under all three wheels. 2) Fix perspective and craft — give the wheels slight elliptical foreshortening consistent with the three-quarter angle, align the canopy edge to the windshield frame, redraw the handlebars as a legible column + grips + steering head, add ambient occlusion under the canopy and a rim light on the near side, and give the cabin windows two-tone depth (frame, glass, seat silhouettes). 3) Deliver the required ornament and street liveliness — add small painted motifs on the front and side panels (e.g., a swirl or 'Om'), a marigold tassel/garland at the headlamp or mirror, a small bell, and a colored trim strip, keeping teal/orange as the base and adding marigold/cream accents; enrich the dark stage with a faint warm floor gradient so the palette feels street-inspired without losing the studio mood. 4) Systematize the annotations — give every callout a consistent thin leader line with an anchor dot on the part, order the numbers front-to-back or clockwise, move labels into the margins at slightly lower opacity so the vehicle stays dominant, and verify no clipping at the viewport edges. 5) Final polish pass — check gradient continuity on the roof and body, unify each mudguard arc with its tire, and confirm the header meta and logo align with the canvas grid.
